summary.text: Earth's radiation balance, also called its energy balance, is the match between the energy Earth gets from the Sun and the energy it loses to space.
Earth keeps a fairly steady temperature because it gives off about as much energy to space as it receives, shifted to longer wavelengths.
Greenhouse gases change how readily heat escapes, so adding them makes surface temperatures rise until absorbed sunlight again equals outgoing radiation.

items.prompt: Earth bathes in sunlight every day, yet it does not keep getting hotter year after year. Why?

options.label: The Sun's output drops a bit each night
It sends out about as much energy as it gets
The oceans store the extra heat forever
Most sunlight never reaches the planet

items.explain: With little net gain or loss, Earth radiates about as much energy to space as it receives, so its temperature stays relatively constant.

items.prompt: Earth sends out more energy than it takes in for many years. What follows?
items.explain: Global cooling takes place when the outgoing energy is greater than the incoming energy.

items.prompt: Some heat from the ground shoots straight out to space without being caught by the air. Where does that happen?

options.label: Only above the poles in winter
Only through gaps in the ozone

items.explain: Thermal radiation in the atmospheric window passes through the atmosphere unimpeded and escapes directly to space.

items.prompt: Energy can hitch a ride upward from the surface in different ways. Which is one way heat is carried into the atmosphere?

options.label: Water evaporating from land and plants
Magnetic currents rising from the core

items.explain: Heat moves into the atmosphere through evapotranspiration and latent heat, conduction and convection, and radiation.

items.prompt: An object's heat output grows with the fourth power of its temperature. What does that mean for Earth's balance?

options.label: Large swings are needed to restore balance
Balance can never be restored once lost
Temperature has no effect on heat output

items.explain: The strong fourth-power sensitivity keeps outgoing energy close to incoming energy through small changes in the planet's temperature.

items.prompt: People run power plants, cars and factories. How does all that energy compare with the heat flowing up from Earth's interior?
items.explain: Geothermal heat flow is about 47 TW, while human energy production is even lower at about 18 TW.

beats.explain: More greenhouse gas cuts outgoing longwave radiation and creates a warming imbalance; surface temperatures rise until absorbed solar radiation equals outgoing longwave radiation again.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Sunlight reaches the top of the atmosphere at an intensity called the solar constant.
Earth catches that sunlight across its cross-section, a circle.
A sphere's surface area is twice that circle's area, so the global average is half the solar constant.
Averaged over the globe and the year, that gives about 340 W/m².

beats.explain: A sphere's surface area is four times its cross-sectional area, so the average is one quarter of the solar constant, about 340 W/m².

beats.idea: Earth stays near a steady temperature by sending out about as much energy as it absorbs, and greenhouse gases shift where that balance settles.

paragraphs.heading: Energy in, energy out
paragraphs.text: Earth's energy balance, also called its energy budget, compares the energy that arrives from the Sun with the energy Earth loses to space. Other sources, such as heat from Earth's interior, are counted too, but they are tiny next to sunlight. Huge amounts of energy flow in and out, yet Earth's temperature stays fairly steady because, overall, it gains or loses little. It sends out to space about as much energy as it takes in, only at longer wavelengths.

paragraphs.heading: How sunlight arrives
paragraphs.text: The energy reaching the top of the atmosphere each second equals the solar constant times Earth's cross-sectional area facing the Sun. A sphere's surface is four times the area of its cross-section. So, averaged over the whole globe and the year, the incoming flow is a quarter of the solar constant, roughly 340 watts per square meter (W/m²). Absorption changes with place, time of day, season and year, so figures like this are averages over many years of satellite readings.

paragraphs.heading: How heat leaves
paragraphs.text: Energy leaves as outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), the thermal radiation given off by Earth's surface and atmosphere. A wavelength of 4 microns is sometimes used as the dividing line between longwave and shortwave. Part of the solar energy absorbed by the ground is given off again at wavelengths in the atmospheric window, which pass straight through the air to space. The rest is carried upward by evapotranspiration and latent heat, by conduction and convection, and by radiation, until some of it can escape too. In the end, all energy leaving Earth goes out as longwave radiation.

paragraphs.heading: Why the balance holds
paragraphs.text: The atmosphere has an emissivity, written ε, that is below 1 because the air does not emit in the atmospheric window. Aerosols, clouds, water vapor and trace greenhouse gases together give it an effective value of about ε = 0.78. Outgoing energy is very sensitive to temperature, rising with its fourth power. That means small shifts in the planet's temperature are enough to keep the outgoing flow close to the incoming one.

paragraphs.heading: When greenhouse gases change
paragraphs.text: Seen from space, greenhouse gases change the planet's emissivity, so altering what the air is made of can shift the radiation balance. More greenhouse gas traps more heat, an enhanced greenhouse effect, which lowers OLR and leaves Earth with a warming imbalance. Surface temperatures then climb until absorbed solar radiation (ASR) once again equals OLR. The same works in reverse when greenhouse gases fall: temperatures drop until the two match.

paragraphs.heading: Warming and cooling
paragraphs.text: When the incoming and outgoing flows match, Earth is in radiative equilibrium and its climate stays fairly stable. More energy coming in than going out means global warming; more going out than coming in means global cooling. Many kinds of measurement show a warming imbalance since at least 1970. Its main source is human-made change to the makeup of the atmosphere.
